title: Reference
text:
Data
Daily simulated wheat growth from the APSIM model at Narrabri (NSW, Australia): 199 genotypes, 31 seasons (1983 to 2013). See Data for the columns. Files are in data/.
The data are simulation output. The source and licence of the underlying APSIM simulations should be confirmed before reuse or redistribution; this repository grants no licence for them.

title: Reference
text:
Sources

Brunton, S. L., Proctor, J. L. and Kutz, J. N. (2016). Discovering governing equations from data by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamical systems. PNAS 113(15), 3932–3937.
Bustos-Korts, D. et al. (2019). From QTLs to adaptation landscapes: using genotype-to-phenotype models to characterize G×E over time. Frontiers in Plant Science 10, 1540. doi:10.3389/fpls.2019.01540
Apley, D. W. and Zhu, J. (2020). Visualizing the effects of predictor variables in black box supervised learning models. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 82(4), 1059–1086.

title: 8 · Limitations
text:
The same pipeline is applied to leaf area index (LAI), which rises and then falls during the season, by changing var = "lai".

trl <- make_trajectories(traj, drv, var = "lai")
gl  <- gram_stats(Theta, trl)
cvl <- cv_blocked(Theta, trl, gl, fit_ols)

As an alternative library, a B-spline basis in thermal time with the other three drivers entering linearly:

df <- 6; TT <- drv$U[, , 1]; B <- bs(as.vector(TT), df = df)
Th_spl <- array(NA_real_, c(dim(TT), 1 + df + 3), dimnames = list(NULL, NULL, c("1", paste0("B", 1:df), "DL", "RAW", "RAD")))
Th_spl[, , 1] <- 1
for (j in 1:df) Th_spl[, , 1 + j] <- B[, j]
for (j in 1:3)  Th_spl[, , 1 + df + j] <- drv$U[, , j + 1]
cvs <- cv_blocked(Th_spl, trl, gram_stats(Th_spl, trl), fit_ols)

lookup_all <- function(tr_) {
  base <- array(NA_real_, dim(tr_$Y))
  for (y in seq_along(tr_$years)) base[, y, ] <- apply(tr_$Y[, -y, , drop = FALSE], c(1, 3), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  for (g in 1:dim(base)[1]) for (y in 1:dim(base)[2]) {
    v <- base[g, y, ]; ok <- which(!is.nan(v)); v[is.nan(v)] <- v[max(ok)]; base[g, y, ] <- v; base[g, y, 1] <- tr_$Y[g, y, 1] }
  base
}
lk <- lookup_all(trl)
res <- rbind(`cubic polynomial` = evaluate(cvl$pred, trl), `B-spline in TT` = evaluate(cvs$pred, trl), `baseline (no weather)` = evaluate(lk, trl))
round(res, 3)

                      trajectory_rmse fixed_day_rmse maturity_rmse
cubic polynomial                0.885          1.212         0.972
B-spline in TT                  0.526          0.664         0.539
baseline (no weather)           0.473          0.687         0.637



err_by_day <- function(P) sapply(2:dim(P)[3], function(d) { ok <- !is.na(trl$Y[, , d]); sqrt(mean((P[, , d][ok] - trl$Y[, , d][ok])^2)) })
nd <- dim(trl$Y)[3] - 1; lv <- c("cubic polynomial", "B-spline in TT", "baseline")
d <- data.frame(das = rep(2:(nd + 1) + trl$das0 - 1, 3), rmse = c(err_by_day(cvl$pred), err_by_day(cvs$pred), err_by_day(lk)),
                model = factor(rep(lv, each = nd), lv))
d <- d[d$das <= 15 + 140, ]
ggplot(d, aes(das, rmse, colour = model)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(dgxe[c("burgundy", "blue", "grey")])) +
  labs(x = "days after sowing", y = "held-out LAI RMSE") + theme_dgxe() + theme(legend.position = "top", legend.title = element_blank())








A cubic polynomial in the standardised drivers cannot represent the rise and fall of LAI, and its error is larger than that of the baseline throughout. The spline library is considerably better, but over whole trajectories the baseline remains slightly more accurate (0.47 against 0.53); the spline model is better at day 113 and at maturity. When the model is inaccurate, the library should be examined before the fitting method.

title: 8 · Limitations
text:
Collinear drivers
Thermal time and day length have a correlation of 0.97. Fitting the same model separately to odd and even seasons gives different coefficients but nearly identical growth rates.

odd <- which(tr$years %% 2 == 1); even <- which(tr$years %% 2 == 0)
fo <- fit_years(gram, odd, fit_ols); fe <- fit_years(gram, even, fit_ols)
tab <- round(cbind(odd_years = fo$mu, even_years = fe$mu), 3); rownames(tab) <- gram$names
tab[c("TT", "TT^2", "DL", "DL^2"), ]

     odd_years even_years
TT      -0.063     -0.037
TT^2    -0.036     -0.031
DL       0.045      0.020
DL^2    -0.055     -0.051

Tbar <- apply(Theta, c(2, 3), mean)
r_odd <- as.vector(Tbar %*% fo$mu); r_even <- as.vector(Tbar %*% fe$mu)
c(correlation = cor(r_odd, r_even), max_difference = max(abs(r_odd - r_even)))

   correlation max_difference 
   0.998197498    0.009107564 


The data determine the combined effect of correlated drivers better than each coefficient, so response curves are preferable to individual coefficients for interpretation.

title: 8 · Limitations
text:
Accumulation of error
The regression is performed on daily increments, whereas the prediction is their cumulative sum. A small bias in the daily increment therefore accumulates.

cv <- cv_blocked(Theta, tr, gram, fit_ssr, k = 12)
inc_err <- numeric(0)
for (g in seq_along(tr$genotypes)) for (y in seq_along(tr$years)) { n <- tr$nend[g, y]
  inc_err <- c(inc_err, diff(cv$pred[g, y, 1:(n + 1)]) - diff(tr$Y[g, y, 1:(n + 1)])) }
c(daily_increment_rmse = sqrt(mean(inc_err^2)), trajectory_rmse = unname(evaluate(cv$pred, tr)[1]))

daily_increment_rmse      trajectory_rmse 
          0.02801567           0.52096960 


For this reason the model is assessed on the simulated trajectory and not on the daily increments.

title: 6 · Interpretation
text:
For interpretation the model is fitted once to all seasons. The shared coefficients on the 12-term support, in standardised drivers, are:

f  <- fit_years(gram, seq_along(tr$years), fit_ssr, k = 12)
mu <- f$mu
round(setNames(mu[f$support], f$names[f$support]), 4)

      1      TT    TT^2    TT^3      DL    DL^2    DL^3     RAW   RAW^2     RAD 
 0.1551 -0.0355 -0.0290  0.0116  0.0191 -0.0538  0.0184  0.0110 -0.0127  0.0073 
  RAD^2   RAD^3 
-0.0025 -0.0004 

rate <- function(Z) as.vector(library_matrix(Z) %*% mu)

Individual coefficients of a polynomial are difficult to interpret, so the equation is examined through the growth rate it implies.

title: 6 · Interpretation
text:
Growth rate over the season
Predicted growth rate for the weather of each season (grey) and the mean (blue).

ny <- length(tr$years); nd <- dim(Theta)[2]
R  <- sapply(seq_len(ny), function(y) as.vector(Theta[y, , ] %*% mu))
d  <- data.frame(das = rep(seq_len(nd) + tr$das0 - 1, ny), year = rep(tr$years, each = nd), rate = as.vector(R))
d  <- d[d$das <= 15 + max(tr$nend) - 1, ]
ggplot(d, aes(das, rate)) + geom_line(aes(group = year), colour = dgxe[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", colour = dgxe[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "days after sowing", y = "growth rate (t/ha/day)") + theme_dgxe()

title: 6 · Interpretation
text:
Effect of a single driver
The effect of one driver cannot be read by varying it alone while the others are held fixed, since the drivers are correlated in real weather:

Z <- observed_points(drv, tr)
round(cor(Z), 2)

       TT    DL   RAW   RAD
TT   1.00  0.97 -0.65  0.72
DL   0.97  1.00 -0.67  0.74
RAW -0.65 -0.67  1.00 -0.58
RAD  0.72  0.74 -0.58  1.00


Accumulated local effects (ALE) vary the driver only within narrow intervals around values that occur, using the observed values of the other drivers, and accumulate the resulting changes in the rate.
ale_curve <- function(rate, Z, j, K = 24) {
  e <- unique(quantile(Z[, j], seq(0, 1, length.out = K + 1))); nb_ <- length(e) - 1
  b <- pmin(pmax(findInterval(Z[, j], e), 1), nb_)
  Zu <- Z; Zl <- Z; Zu[, j] <- e[b + 1]; Zl[, j] <- e[b]
  d <- rate(Zu) - rate(Zl); nb <- tabulate(b, nb_)
  md <- vapply(split(d, factor(b, levels = seq_len(nb_))), sum, 0) / pmax(nb, 1)
  A <- c(0, cumsum(md)); mid <- (A[-1] + A[-length(A)]) / 2
  data.frame(z = e, effect = A - sum(mid * nb) / sum(nb))
}

curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(drv$drivers), function(j) {
  a <- ale_curve(rate, Z, j)
  data.frame(driver = drv$drivers[j], x = a$z * drv$scale[j] + drv$center[j], effect = a$effect)
}))
pts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(drv$drivers), function(j)
  data.frame(driver = drv$drivers[j], x = Z[, j] * drv$scale[j] + drv$center[j])))
curves$driver <- factor(curves$driver, drv$drivers); pts$driver <- factor(pts$driver, drv$drivers)


ggplot(curves, aes(x, effect)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#D1D5DB", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(colour = dgxe[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_rug(data = pts, aes(x = x), inherit.aes = FALSE, sides = "b", alpha = 0.03, colour = dgxe[["ink"]]) +
  facet_wrap(~driver, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "TT (°C d) · DL (h) · RAW (0 to 1) · RAD (MJ/m²/day)", y = "effect on growth rate (t/ha/day)") + theme_dgxe()








The rug marks show where data exist. Thermal time is accumulated from sowing, so its curve describes the dependence of growth on the stage of the season, not a response to temperature. TT and DL are correlated at 0.97 and are best read together.

title: 6 · Interpretation
text:
Interactions and partial dependence
The 13-term library is additive in the drivers, so partial dependence and ALE coincide. With products of drivers (37 terms) they differ:

pdp <- function(rate, Z, j, grid) sapply(grid, function(v) { Zv <- Z; Zv[, j] <- v; mean(rate(Zv)) })
Theta2 <- make_library(drv, pairs = TRUE); gram2 <- gram_stats(Theta2, tr)
f2 <- fit_years(gram2, seq_along(tr$years), fit_ssr, k = 20)
rate2 <- function(Z) as.vector(library_matrix(Z, pairs = TRUE) %*% f2$mu)
curves2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(j) {
  a <- ale_curve(rate2, Z, j); p <- pdp(rate2, Z, j, a$z); x <- a$z * drv$scale[j] + drv$center[j]
  rbind(data.frame(driver = drv$drivers[j], x = x, effect = a$effect, method = "ALE"),
        data.frame(driver = drv$drivers[j], x = x, effect = p - mean(p), method = "partial dependence")) }))


ggplot(curves2, aes(x, effect, colour = method, linetype = method)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + facet_wrap(~driver, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(dgxe[c("blue", "burgundy")])) +
  labs(x = "driver value", y = "effect on growth rate (t/ha/day)") + theme_dgxe() + theme(legend.position = "top", legend.title = element_blank())








Partial dependence evaluates the model at combinations of drivers that do not occur in the data (for example a short day late in a high thermal-time season), whereas ALE does not.

title: 4 · Fitting
text:
For this step all genotypes and seasons are pooled. The statistics are summed and the library columns scaled to unit root-mean-square, so that coefficients are comparable.

st <- sum_years(gram, seq_along(tr$years))
A  <- apply(st$A, c(2, 3), sum)
b  <- colSums(st$b)
sc <- scale_gram(A, b, n = sum(st$n))
terms <- gram$names

title: 4 · Fitting
text:
For this step all genotypes and seasons are pooled. The statistics are summed and the library columns scaled to unit root-mean-square, so that coefficients are comparable.

st <- sum_years(gram, seq_along(tr$years))
A  <- apply(st$A, c(2, 3), sum)
b  <- colSums(st$b)
sc <- scale_gram(A, b, n = sum(st$n))
terms <- gram$names

title: 4 · Fitting
text:
Fitting methods
Each method takes (A, b) and returns list(coef, support).
fit_ols <- function(A, b, ...) {
  list(coef = solve(A, b), support = seq_along(b))
}
fit_ridge <- function(A, b, lambda = 0.01, ...) {
  list(coef = solve(A + lambda * mean(diag(A)) * diag(nrow(A)), b), support = seq_along(b))
}
fit_ssr <- function(A, b, k = 8, alpha = 1e-6, ...) {
  S <- seq_along(b)
  repeat {
    co <- solve(A[S, S, drop = FALSE] + alpha * diag(length(S)), b[S])
    if (length(S) <= k) break
    S <- S[-which.min(abs(co))]
  }
  coef <- numeric(length(b)); coef[S] <- co
  list(coef = coef, support = S)
}

ols <- fit_ols(sc$A, sc$b)
rdg <- fit_ridge(sc$A, sc$b, lambda = 0.01)
ssr <- fit_ssr(sc$A, sc$b, k = 8)
tab <- data.frame(term = terms, OLS = ols$coef, ridge = rdg$coef, SSR_8 = ssr$coef)
tab[, -1] <- round(tab[, -1], 3)
tab

    term    OLS  ridge  SSR_8
1      1  0.156  0.143  0.154
2     TT -0.034  0.002 -0.016
3   TT^2 -0.032 -0.033 -0.030
4   TT^3  0.018  0.005  0.011
5     DL  0.019 -0.007  0.002
6   DL^2 -0.055 -0.040 -0.056
7   DL^3  0.024  0.020  0.026
8    RAW  0.011  0.009  0.000
9  RAW^2 -0.017 -0.015 -0.020
10 RAW^3 -0.001  0.002  0.000
11   RAD  0.007  0.008  0.000
12 RAD^2 -0.003 -0.003  0.000
13 RAD^3 -0.001 -0.002  0.000



d <- reshape(tab, direction = "long", varying = list(2:4), v.names = "coef", timevar = "method", times = names(tab)[2:4], idvar = "term")
d$term <- factor(d$term, rev(terms)); d$method <- factor(d$method, names(tab)[2:4])
ggplot(d, aes(coef, term, colour = method, shape = method)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#D1D5DB", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(dgxe[c("blue", "grey", "burgundy")])) +
  labs(x = "coefficient (scaled library)", y = NULL) + theme_dgxe() + theme(legend.position = "top", legend.title = element_blank())

title: 4 · Fitting
text:
Order of elimination
Sequential thresholding removes one term at a time; the order is the following.

S <- seq_along(terms); out <- character(0)
while (length(S) > 1) {
  co <- solve(sc$A[S, S, drop = FALSE] + 1e-6 * diag(length(S)), sc$b[S])
  w <- which.min(abs(co)); out <- c(out, terms[S[w]]); S <- S[-w]
}
c(removed = out, last = terms[S])

 removed1  removed2  removed3  removed4  removed5  removed6  removed7  removed8 
  "RAW^3"   "RAD^3"   "RAD^2"     "RAD"     "RAW"      "DL"    "TT^3"      "TT" 
 removed9 removed10 removed11 removed12      last 
  "RAW^2"    "DL^3"    "DL^2"    "TT^2"       "1" 


The order depends on the library and on correlations among its terms, and is not a ranking of importance. The number of terms is chosen by validation (step 5).

title: 4 · Fitting
2 · Data
text:
The data are APSIM simulations of wheat at Narrabri (New South Wales): 199 genotypes in 31 seasons (1983 to 2013), daily from 15 days after sowing to maturity. Weather is common to all genotypes within a season and is stored in a separate table.
wx   <- read.csv("data/narrabri_weather.csv")
traj <- read.csv("data/narrabri_biomass.csv.gz")
head(wx, 3)

title: 2 · Data
text:
Biomass
Each line is one genotype. The four seasons were chosen to span the range of weather.

sel <- traj[traj$year %in% c(1984, 1990, 1998, 2008), ]
ggplot(sel, aes(das, biomass, group = genotype)) + geom_line(colour = dgxe[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~year, nrow = 1) + labs(x = "days after sowing", y = "biomass (t/ha)") + theme_dgxe()

title: 2 · Data
text:
Weather
Each grey line is one season; the blue line is the mean over seasons.

w <- reshape(wx, direction = "long", varying = c("TT", "DL", "RAW", "RAD"), v.names = "value", timevar = "driver",
             times = c("TT", "DL", "RAW", "RAD"), idvar = c("year", "das"))
w$driver <- factor(w$driver, c("TT", "DL", "RAW", "RAD"))
m <- aggregate(value ~ driver + das, w, mean)
ggplot(w, aes(das, value)) + geom_line(aes(group = year), colour = dgxe[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.25, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = m, colour = dgxe[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.8) + facet_wrap(~driver, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "days after sowing", y = NULL) + theme_dgxe()








Trajectories end on different days, since genotypes mature at different times. The end of each trajectory is tracked in step 3.

title: Set up
text:

title: Set up

Packages
R 4.1 or later. The modelling code uses base R only. The figures use ggplot2:
install.packages("ggplot2")

title: Set up
text:
Test run
source("R/functions.R")

wx   <- read.csv("data/narrabri_weather.csv")
traj <- read.csv("data/narrabri_biomass.csv.gz")

drv   <- make_drivers(wx)
Theta <- make_library(drv)
tr    <- make_trajectories(traj, drv)
gram  <- gram_stats(Theta, tr)

cv <- cv_blocked(Theta, tr, gram, fit_ssr, k = 12)
round(evaluate(cv$pred, tr), 3)
The expected output is a trajectory RMSE of about 0.52 t/ha. The research implementation in Python gives 0.520, 0.688 and 0.749 for the trajectory, day-113 and maturity RMSE; this code gives 0.521, 0.689 and 0.747.

title: Sparse identification of crop growth dynamics
text:
This workshop fits a daily growth equation for wheat biomass to simulated field-trial data, using base R. The growth rate is written as a sparse combination of candidate functions of the weather (SINDy), the coefficients are obtained by regression, and the resulting equation is validated on years that were not used for fitting.
The data are APSIM simulations for one site (Narrabri): 199 genotypes, 31 seasons (1983 to 2013), daily resolution. Each step below is a short function with a defined input and output, so that any step, in particular the regression method, can be replaced independently of the others.



Step
Content




Set up
Files, packages, a test run


1 · Method
Model, regression formulation, solution, validation


2 · Data
Weather and biomass tables


3 · Library and design matrix
Candidate functions, design matrix, normal equations


4 · Fitting
OLS, ridge, sequential thresholding, lasso


5 · Validation
Simulation and leave-one-year-out cross-validation


6 · Interpretation
Response curves


7 · Genotypes
Shared coefficients and genotype deviations; ranking


8 · Limitations
Library choice, collinearity, error accumulation


9 · Extensions
Coupled states and further directions


Reference
Symbols, functions, data, sources



All functions are in R/functions.R and use base R only; ggplot2 is used for the figures. The full pipeline, including cross-validation over all genotypes, runs in a few seconds.
The data are simulation output from APSIM (Bustos-Korts et al., 2019). The source and licence should be confirmed before reuse.



 Back to top

title: 1 · Method
text:
Let \(y(t)\) denote biomass and \(u(t) = (\mathrm{TT}, \mathrm{DL}, \mathrm{RAW}, \mathrm{RAD})\) the daily weather drivers: accumulated thermal time, day length, relative available water and solar radiation. The growth rate is modelled as
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t} = \sum_{j=1}^{K} \xi_j\,\theta_j\bigl(u(t)\bigr),
\]
where \(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_K\) is a fixed library of candidate functions and \(\xi\) is a vector of coefficients. The library used here contains a constant and the first three powers of each driver (\(K=13\)).

title: 1 · Method
text:
Let \(y(t)\) denote biomass and \(u(t) = (\mathrm{TT}, \mathrm{DL}, \mathrm{RAW}, \mathrm{RAD})\) the daily weather drivers: accumulated thermal time, day length, relative available water and solar radiation. The growth rate is modelled as
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t} = \sum_{j=1}^{K} \xi_j\,\theta_j\bigl(u(t)\bigr),
\]
where \(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_K\) is a fixed library of candidate functions and \(\xi\) is a vector of coefficients. The library used here contains a constant and the first three powers of each driver (\(K=13\)).

title: 1 · Method
text:
Regression
With daily data, the increments \(z_t = y_{t+1}-y_t\) are regressed on the library evaluated at day \(t\). Because \(\xi\) enters linearly, this is an ordinary linear least-squares problem
\[
\min_{\xi}\ \lVert z - X\xi\rVert_2^2, \qquad X_{tj} = \theta_j(u_t).
\]
The data enter only through \(A = X^\top X\) and \(b = X^\top z\). These are computed once per genotype and season, so that cross-validation reduces to adding and subtracting small matrices. Every fitting method in step 4 has the signature fit(A, b, ...).

title: 1 · Method
text:
Sparsity
Sequential thresholding refits the model and removes the term with the smallest scaled coefficient until \(k\) terms remain. The retained set of terms (the support) is common to all genotypes.

title: 1 · Method
text:
Genotypes
The coefficients of genotype \(g\) are \(\xi_g = \mu + \delta_g\). The shared part \(\mu\) is estimated from all genotypes on the common support, and each deviation \(\delta_g\) is estimated from the data of genotype \(g\) with a ridge penalty.

title: 1 · Method
text:
Solution
Since the library depends on the weather only, the equation can be solved by a cumulative sum, without an ODE solver:
\[
y(t) = y_0 + \sum_{s<t} \sum_j \xi_j\,\theta_j(u_s).
\]

title: 1 · Method
text:
Validation
Seasons are the independent units, because the weather of neighbouring days is strongly correlated. The model is validated by leave-one-year-out cross-validation: each year is predicted from a model fitted to the other 30, starting from the mean initial biomass.

title: 1 · Method
3 · Library and design matrix
text:
Each driver is standardised to mean 0 and unit standard deviation. Only weather is used in this step; the response does not enter.
make_drivers <- function(wx, drivers = c("TT", "DL", "RAW", "RAD")) {
  years <- sort(unique(wx$year)); das0 <- min(wx$das); nd <- max(wx$das) - das0 + 1
  U <- array(NA_real_, c(length(years), nd, length(drivers)), dimnames = list(years, NULL, drivers))
  for (i in seq_along(years)) {
    w <- wx[wx$year == years[i], ]
    U[i, w$das - das0 + 1, ] <- as.matrix(w[, drivers])
    last <- max(w$das) - das0 + 1                       # years end on different days:
    if (last < nd) U[i, (last + 1):nd, ] <- matrix(rep(U[i, last, ], each = nd - last), nd - last)  # carry last value (never used)
  }
  center <- apply(U, 3, mean); scale <- apply(U, 3, function(x) sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2)))
  for (j in seq_along(drivers)) U[, , j] <- (U[, , j] - center[j]) / scale[j]
  list(U = U, years = years, das0 = das0, drivers = drivers, center = center, scale = scale)
}

title: 3 · Library and design matrix
3 · Library and design matrix
text:
Response
The response is stored as an array Y[genotype, year, day], with NA after maturity. The number of daily steps of each trajectory is kept in nend.
make_trajectories <- function(traj, drv, var = "biomass") {
  gen <- sort(unique(traj$genotype)); nd <- dim(drv$U)[2]
  Y <- array(NA_real_, c(length(gen), length(drv$years), nd), dimnames = list(gen, drv$years, NULL))
  Y[cbind(match(traj$genotype, gen), match(traj$year, drv$years), traj$das - drv$das0 + 1)] <- traj[[var]]
  nend <- apply(Y, c(1, 2), function(v) sum(!is.na(v)) - 1)
  list(Y = Y, nend = nend, genotypes = gen, years = drv$years, das0 = drv$das0)
}

title: 3 · Library and design matrix
text:
Design matrix
The increments \(z_t = y_{t+1} - y_t\) are regressed on the library at day \(t\). For three genotypes:
build_design <- function(Theta, tr, genotypes = tr$genotypes) {
  X <- list(); z <- list(); id <- list()
  for (g in genotypes) for (y in seq_along(tr$years)) {
    gi <- match(g, tr$genotypes); n <- tr$nend[gi, y]; v <- tr$Y[gi, y, 1:(n + 1)]
    X[[length(X) + 1]] <- matrix(Theta[y, 1:n, ], n); z[[length(z) + 1]] <- diff(v)
    id[[length(id) + 1]] <- data.frame(genotype = g, year = tr$years[y], day = 0:(n - 1))
  }
  X <- do.call(rbind, X); colnames(X) <- dimnames(Theta)[[3]]
  list(X = X, z = unlist(z), id = do.call(rbind, id))
}

title: 3 · Library and design matrix
text:
Normal equations
A linear fit needs only \(A = X^\top X\) and \(b = X^\top z\). These are computed per genotype and season, avoiding the full design matrix (about 850,000 rows for all genotypes).
gram_stats <- function(Theta, tr) {
  G <- dim(tr$Y)[1]; ny <- length(tr$years); K <- dim(Theta)[3]
  A <- array(0, c(G, ny, K, K)); b <- array(0, c(G, ny, K))
  for (g in seq_len(G)) for (y in seq_len(ny)) {
    n <- tr$nend[g, y]; X <- matrix(Theta[y, 1:n, ], n)
    A[g, y, , ] <- crossprod(X); b[g, y, ] <- crossprod(X, diff(tr$Y[g, y, 1:(n + 1)]))
  }
  list(A = A, b = b, n = tr$nend, names = dimnames(Theta)[[3]])
}

gram <- gram_stats(Theta, tr)
A <- apply(gram$A[1:3, , , ], c(3, 4), sum); b <- apply(gram$b[1:3, , ], 3, sum)
c(max_diff_A = max(abs(A - crossprod(des$X))), max_diff_b = max(abs(b - crossprod(des$X, des$z))))

  max_diff_A   max_diff_b 
4.569301e-09 2.160050e-12 

max(abs(solve(A, b) - coef(lm(des$z ~ des$X - 1))))

[1] 5.162537e-15

title: 5 · Validation
text:
Leave-one-year-out cross-validation
The same procedure is repeated for each of the 31 seasons.
cv_blocked <- function(Theta, tr, gram, fitter = fit_ssr, k = 12, lam_mu = 1e-4, lam_g = 0.01, ...) {
  ny <- length(tr$years); G <- length(tr$genotypes); nd <- dim(Theta)[2]
  P <- array(NA_real_, c(G, ny, nd)); S_all <- vector("list", ny)
  for (yv in seq_len(ny)) {
    train <- setdiff(seq_len(ny), yv); f <- fit_years(gram, train, fitter, k, lam_mu, lam_g, ...)
    y0 <- apply(tr$Y[, train, 1, drop = FALSE], 1, mean)                        # initial biomass: mean of training years
    P[, yv, ] <- t(simulate(f$xi, Theta[yv, , ], y0)); S_all[[yv]] <- f$support
  }
  list(pred = P, support = S_all)
}
evaluate <- function(P, tr, fixed_day = 99) {
  G <- dim(P)[1]; ny <- dim(P)[2]; se <- 0; cnt <- 0; fin <- numeric(0)
  for (g in seq_len(G)) for (y in seq_len(ny)) {
    n <- tr$nend[g, y]; d <- 2:(n + 1)                      # day index 1..n (day 0 is the given start)
    se <- se + sum((P[g, y, d] - tr$Y[g, y, d])^2); cnt <- cnt + length(d)
    fin <- c(fin, P[g, y, n + 1] - tr$Y[g, y, n + 1])
  }
  c(trajectory_rmse = sqrt(se / cnt), fixed_day_rmse = sqrt(mean((P[, , fixed_day] - tr$Y[, , fixed_day])^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
    maturity_rmse = sqrt(mean(fin^2)))
}

title: 5 · Validation
text:
Baseline without weather
As a reference, each trajectory is predicted by the mean curve of the same genotype in the other seasons.

base <- array(NA_real_, dim(tr$Y))
for (y in seq_along(tr$years)) base[, y, ] <- apply(tr$Y[, -y, , drop = FALSE], c(1, 3), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
for (g in 1:dim(base)[1]) for (y in 1:dim(base)[2]) {
  v <- base[g, y, ]; ok <- which(!is.nan(v)); v[is.nan(v)] <- v[max(ok)]      # hold the last mean after the last other season ends
  base[g, y, ] <- v; base[g, y, 1] <- tr$Y[g, y, 1]
}

Choice of fitting method
All methods share the signature fit(A, b, ...), so they can be compared in one loop.

res <- cached("swap_methods.rds", do.call(rbind, lapply(names(methods), function(nm) {
  m <- methods[[nm]]; cv <- do.call(cv_blocked, c(list(Theta, tr, gram, m[[1]]), m[-1]))
  data.frame(method = nm, t(round(evaluate(cv$pred, tr), 3))) })))

Number of terms

title: 7 · Genotypes
text:
The coefficients of genotype \(g\) are \(\xi_g = \mu + \delta_g\). The support is common to all genotypes. The shared vector \(\mu\) is estimated from the pooled data; each \(\delta_g\) is a ridge-penalised correction estimated from the data of genotype \(g\) only.
fit_hier <- function(Ag, bg, support, lam_mu = 1e-4, lam_g = 0.01) {
  K <- dim(Ag)[2]; k <- length(support); G <- dim(Ag)[1]
  Apool <- apply(Ag[, support, support, drop = FALSE], c(2, 3), sum); bpool <- colSums(bg[, support, drop = FALSE])
  mu <- numeric(K); mu[support] <- solve(Apool + lam_mu * mean(diag(Apool)) * diag(k), bpool)
  delta <- matrix(0, G, K)
  for (g in seq_len(G)) {
    Aq <- Ag[g, support, support]; tr <- sum(diag(Aq)) / k
    delta[g, support] <- solve(Aq + lam_g * tr * diag(k), bg[g, support] - Aq %*% mu[support])
  }
  list(mu = mu, delta = delta, xi = sweep(delta, 2, mu, "+"), support = support)
}

f <- fit_years(gram, seq_along(tr$years), fit_ssr, k = 12)
dim(f$xi)

title: 7 · Genotypes

The coefficients of genotype \(g\) are \(\xi_g = \mu + \delta_g\). The support is common to all genotypes. The shared vector \(\mu\) is estimated from the pooled data; each \(\delta_g\) is a ridge-penalised correction estimated from the data of genotype \(g\) only.
fit_hier <- function(Ag, bg, support, lam_mu = 1e-4, lam_g = 0.01) {
  K <- dim(Ag)[2]; k <- length(support); G <- dim(Ag)[1]
  Apool <- apply(Ag[, support, support, drop = FALSE], c(2, 3), sum); bpool <- colSums(bg[, support, drop = FALSE])
  mu <- numeric(K); mu[support] <- solve(Apool + lam_mu * mean(diag(Apool)) * diag(k), bpool)
  delta <- matrix(0, G, K)
  for (g in seq_len(G)) {
    Aq <- Ag[g, support, support]; tr <- sum(diag(Aq)) / k
    delta[g, support] <- solve(Aq + lam_g * tr * diag(k), bg[g, support] - Aq %*% mu[support])

title: 7 · Genotypes
text:
Ranking genotypes
For each season the predicted and APSIM biomass of the 199 genotypes at a fixed day are compared by the Spearman correlation and by the overlap of the top 10%. The reference is the mean of the genotype in the other seasons.
rank_scores <- function(Pd, Yd, top = 0.1) {
  k <- max(1, round(top * nrow(Yd)))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(ncol(Yd)), function(y) data.frame(
    year = y, rho = cor(Pd[, y], Yd[, y], method = "spearman"),
    top = length(intersect(order(-Pd[, y])[1:k], order(-Yd[, y])[1:k])) / k)))
}
lookup_baseline <- function(Yd) (rowSums(Yd) - Yd) / (ncol(Yd) - 1)

cv   <- cv_blocked(Theta, tr, gram, fit_ssr, k = 12)
days <- c(35, 50, 63, 84, 99)                         # day index; das = index + 14
out  <- do.call(rbind, lapply(days, function(d) {
  Yd <- tr$Y[, , d]; a <- rank_scores(cv$pred[, , d], Yd); b <- rank_scores(lookup_baseline(Yd), Yd)
  data.frame(das = d + tr$das0 - 1, method = c("model", "baseline"),
             rho = c(mean(a$rho), mean(b$rho)), top10 = c(mean(a$top), mean(b$top))) }))
out$rho <- round(out$rho, 3); out$top10 <- round(out$top10, 3); out

Early in the season the baseline ranks genotypes better, since the order is determined mainly by genotype and not yet by weather. From about day 100 the model is better. These results are for genotypes included in fitting and seasons that were held out.

title: 9 · Extensions
text: The numbers and figures on this page come from the research code (Python), not from the R functions of the previous steps, and are not reproduced in R.

title: 9 · Extensions
text:
Coupled states
In steps 4 to 8 the growth rate depends on the weather but not on the state of the crop, so the solution is a cumulative sum. In a crop, a larger leaf area intercepts more light and increases biomass growth. A model with this feedback is a coupled system in leaf area index \(L\) and biomass \(B\),
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}L}{\mathrm{d}t} = f_L(L, B, u_t), \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} = f_B(L, B, u_t),
\]
Because the state appears on the right-hand side, the solution requires numerical integration. The regression remains linear in the coefficients, so steps 3 and 4 apply unchanged, but errors in the states feed back into the rates.

title: 9 · Extensions
text:
Physical terms in the library
A candidate term for biomass growth is the light intercepted by the canopy, \(I = 1 - \exp(-0.5\,L)\), multiplied by radiation: \(\mathrm{d}B/\mathrm{d}t \ni I \cdot \mathrm{RAD}\).

title: 9 · Extensions
text:
Further directions

Other regression methods: any method with the signature fit(A, b, ...). Bayesian regression with sparsity-inducing priors provides uncertainty for the coefficients at higher computational cost.
Several sites: pooling sites adds variation in the weather.
New genotypes: prediction for a genotype not used in fitting requires additional information about it, for example its parameter values. This is not treated here.
Other responses: step 8 shows leaf area index as an example.
